newsitem.title: USA: Consumers spent less, saved more in September.
newsitem.headline: Consumers spent less, saved more in September.

text.p: Consumers held spending in check in September and diverted some of their higher earnings into savings, the government said Thursday, adding to signs of slow but steady economic growth ahead.
The report reflected the sluggish consumer spending for the third quarter as a whole that contributed to slower economic growth in the period, as reported on Wednesday.
Analysts said while consumer spending was likely to pick up in the current quarter -- leading to a reasonably strong Christmas sales season -- the economy overall would probably remain in low gear.
Consumer spending on goods and services rose a scant 0.1 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $5.18 trillion in September, after a 0.5 percent gain in August, the Commerce Department said.
Incomes from wages, salaries and other sources grew 0.6 percent to a $6.54 trillion rate after a 0.5 percent August rise.

"I view the September slowdown in consumer spending primarily as a sign that the consumer was taking somewhat of a breather," said economist Lynn Reaser of Barnett Banks Inc. in Jacksonville, Fla. "But the support is present for a pickup in the fourth quarter."
Reaser said high levels of consumer confidence, strength in the stock market and solid increases in earnings would lead to rising consumer spending in the current quarter.

The department reported on Wednesday that economic growth slowed to a 2.2 percent rate in the third quarter, from a 4.7 percent rate in the second quarter, in large part because consumer spending slowed to a near standstill.

President Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole each tried to put their own spin on Wednesday's report, with the president claiming his policies were fostering sustained expansion while Dole claimed a recession was in the making.

In its report Thursday, the department said savings jumped to 5.7 cents out of each dollar earned in September from 5.2 cents in August, the strongest savings rate since 6.3 cents of each dollar earned was ploughed into savings in December 1993.
Other reports issued Thursday also pointed to strong labour markets that should prop up wages and help consumer spending, analysts said.

The Labour Department said the number of people filing new claims for unemployment pay rose by 26,000 to 342,000 last week, but the figures were inflated by layoffs in the automobile industry related to a strike against General Motors Corp. in Canada that ended Oct. 24.
The average rate of new claims over the past four weeks -- which smooths fluctuations in the more-volatile weekly numbers -- rose just slightly to 331,250 from 331,000 in the prior four-week period.

"Net of strike effects the initial unemployment claims series continues to portray strength in the labour market," said economist Marilyn Schaja of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.
The Federal Reserve, in its latest report on the national economy issued on Wednesday, described national labour markets as "tight" in a survey of the central bank's 12 regional districts.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce said Thursday that its survey of 6,000 member companies showed less optimism in October about economic growth, sales and hiring.

Its business confidence index dipped to 53.5 in October from 54.8 in August, the previous month surveyed. The business lobbying group's vice-president, Martin Regalia, said it confirmed the outlook for slower growth the rest of the year.

"But even with the slowing, the economy should continue to grow at its long-run trend rate," Regalia added, referring to the Fed's rule-of-thumb that the economy can grow at a 2 percent to 2-1/4 percent rate with little risk of fuelling inflation.
A separate report from the Conference Board said its help-wanted advertising index climbed to 84.0 in September from 81.0 in August, another sign of strong demand for labour.
"Job growth, along with rising wage income, could translate into a pickup in consumer spending in the final months of 1996," said Ken Goldstein, economist for the business research group.

In September, spending on durable goods fell to an annual rate of $634.1 billion from $643.2 billion in August, the Commerce Department said. Spending for nondurables like food rose to a rate of $1.55 trillion from $1.54 trillion in August, while spending for services edged up to $2.99 trillion.
